And from there the Franks went down to the Jordan River.
The Arabs, however, when they were distressed by famine,
because they were far from their cities,
departed and went and encamped at the citadel of Damascus.
And on Friday, the emir Mawdud entered the Great Mosque to pray.
And when they finished prayer,
he and the emir Toghtekin were holding each other's hands,
and admiring the wonders of the buildings.
Then a certain man jumped upon Mawdud,
and struck him with a knife four blows.
And when he was carried and brought to Toghtekin's residence,
he ended his life.
And as for the one who killed him,
on that very spot the servants of Mawdud cut him to pieces, limb by limb.
And some suspected
that Ridwan, the lord of Aleppo, had sent the Ismaili.
And others suspected
that Toghtekin himself had prepared the murderer, a certain evil-doer who was imprisoned,
and had promised him great rewards to do this,
because he was afraid for his city from Mawdud.
And when Mawdud died,
there arose in his place as commander-in-chief the emir Aqsunqur Bursuqi,
and he encamped with fifteen thousand [men] against Edessa for two months.
And in the year 1428 [of the Greeks],
508 of the Arabs [= 1114-1115 AD]:
the Franks were constantly sallying forth from Edessa,
and killing some of the Arabs.
One time they went out,
and captured eleven Arab men,
and brought them into the city,
and impaled them upon the wall in the sight of the Turks,
after they had cut off their hands and their feet.
And when this grieved Aqsunqur greatly,
he brought fifty Frankish prisoners and they killed them.
And the Turks were hard pressed by hunger,
and they abandoned Edessa,
and went to Samosata,
over which, and over Marash, Kaysum, and Raban, the wife of Kogh Vasil the Armenian was ruling.
When her husband died, she had administered these regions very wisely,
and she gathered for herself a large force of horsemen and foot soldiers;
for each month she would give twelve gold dinars to a horseman,
and three dinars to a foot soldier.
